name: Parkinson's Law
statement: Work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion.
statementAccent: expands so as to fill the time available
meaning: A task will quietly swell to occupy whatever time you give it. The same job takes an afternoon when it is due at five and a fortnight when it is due in a fortnight.
mechanism: Work has no fixed size; it expands to fill the time allotted because slack invites polishing, second-guessing, and procedural elaboration. A deadline forces prioritisation — it makes the cost of perfectionism visible — which is why the same task finished in a day and in a month can be hard to tell apart.
example: Parkinson's own illustration: an elderly lady of leisure spends an entire day sending one postcard to her niece at Bognor Regis. An hour goes on finding the card, another on hunting for her spectacles, half an hour on searching out the address, an hour and a quarter on composing it, and twenty minutes on deciding whether to take an umbrella to the pillar-box in the next street. A busy person would have posted it on the way to something else.
whyItMatters: Generous deadlines do not buy quality, they buy elaboration. Shorter timeboxes, smaller batches, and a hard question about what would actually be lost by finishing sooner are usually cheaper than more calendar.
misreadings: It is an observation about how effort fills available time, not proof that every deadline should be brutal or that rushed work is always as good. Squeeze too hard and quality does suffer. The useful reading is that generous time is not free — it quietly recruits busywork — so constrain deliberately.
origin: C. Northcote Parkinson, a naval historian, opened a satirical essay in The Economist on 19 November 1955 with this line as a "commonplace observation". The bulk of that essay was actually about something else — his finding that bureaucracies grow at a steady rate regardless of the work to be done, driven by what he called the Law of Multiplication of Subordinates. The essay was expanded into the 1958 book Parkinson's Law: The Pursuit of Progress.

sources.text: Parkinson, C.N. (19 November 1955). "Parkinson's Law." The Economist. — the original essay.
